title: Exploring EFL Secondary Students’ AI-generated Text Editing While Composition Writing
extended_summary:
This paper examines how secondary EFL students actually manipulate AI-generated text while composing an expository essay, addressing a gap in prior research that had focused more on perceptions of AI or overall writing outcomes than on students’ in-process editing behavior. The study asks two questions: what kinds of edits students make to AI-generated text, and what broader patterns characterize how they draft and revise while working with generative AI.

The intervention/context was an AI-assisted writing workshop conducted in Hong Kong secondary schools. Students received a two-hour workshop led by the first author that reviewed either process-based or genre-based writing instruction and introduced prompt engineering using the POE app, which provides access to chatbots such as ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini. Students then worked on an authentic 500-word expository/article writing task in Google Docs, using any combination of self-written and AI-generated text while recording their screens. The analysis combined quantitative content analysis of edits with qualitative thematic and case-based analysis of screen recordings.

Participants were 29 secondary students from seven Hong Kong schools, although only 25 recordings showed AI-generated text edits and were analyzed. Students ranged from grade level one to five in Hong Kong secondary school (approximately ages 12–18), spanning both lower and upper secondary grades. The schools were purposefully selected to include both higher- and lower-achieving schools, but there was no experimental comparison group and no delayed follow-up. The setting appears workshop/classroom-based within schools.

The study identified 15 types of AI-generated text edits across seven categories, including insertion, deletion, replacement, formatting, Apple predictive text, and Google Docs suggestions. The authors conclude that students were not merely pasting AI output passively; instead, they often actively evaluated, modified, and integrated AI-generated text in complex ways. Four editing patterns were identified: planning with top-down drafting/revising, top-down drafting/revising without planning, planning with bottom-up drafting/revising, and bottom-up drafting/revising without planning. For the user’s requested evidence focus, the paper does not report subgroup or moderator analyses by baseline writing proficiency, English learner status variation, disability, gender, grade level, school achievement level, subject area, or writing genre beyond the expository-task context; it also does not report self-efficacy, confidence, metacognition outcomes, follow-up unaided writing after removal of AI feedback, independent revision skill transfer, plagiarism, overreliance, or adverse effects as measured outcomes. The paper discusses agency and authorial voice conceptually, but does not test them as outcomes.
quality_tier_rationale: This is an exploratory mixed-methods study centered on qualitative screen-recording analysis with descriptive counts, no control group, no causal identification strategy, and no standardized outcome measures. It provides useful process evidence but meets only limited causal-credibility criteria.
impact_tier_rationale: The study shows meaningful but unclear descriptive process impacts on how secondary EFL students compose with AI, yet it does not estimate learning gains or report effect sizes. Because impact on writing performance or priority subgroups is not established, overall impact remains unclear.

interventions.use_case: Secondary EFL students used generative AI chatbots via the POE app, alongside AI-assisted writing features in Google Docs and iOS, to generate, insert, revise, and edit text while composing expository drafts.
Students prompted ChatGPT and other chatbots conversationally for ideas, plans, model text, titles, and paragraph-level writing support during expository composition.

finding.finding_summary: In 25 analyzed screen recordings from 29 recruited Hong Kong secondary EFL students, the study identified 266 AI-generated text edits across 15 edit types and four writing-process patterns, showing that students actively inserted, deleted, and replaced AI-generated text while composing expository writing. However, the paper did not measure improvement in writing quality, unaided posttest writing, independent revision skill after tool removal, or delayed transfer; evidence is therefore limited to descriptive process findings rather than causal literacy gains.
finding.measure: Screen-recorded writing-process behaviors during expository composition; frequencies and categories of AI-generated text insertions, deletions, replacements, and planning/drafting patterns

finding.finding_summary: Qualitative thematic analysis suggested students engaged in planning, evaluation, and revision behaviors that the authors interpret as complex cognitive processing rather than passive copying. At the same time, the study did not directly assess metacognition, self-regulation, transfer of independent revision skill, or follow-up performance once AI support was removed, so durable-skill evidence remains inferential and descriptive only.
finding.measure: Qualitative themes from screen recordings and observation notes on planning, top-down vs. bottom-up drafting, and revision behavior

finding.finding_summary: The paper does not directly measure self-efficacy, confidence, writing anxiety, motivation, or related social-emotional outcomes in this sample. Although the discussion mentions student agency and concerns about authorial voice in prior literature, no empirical social-emotional outcome data are reported from the present study.
